abstracts.abstract: We present a novel theoretical framework for understanding meta-learning that fundamentally reconceptualizes how agents acquire rapid adaptation capabilities across task distributions. Existing meta-learning theories suffer from fragmentation, with separate analyses for gradient-based, memory-augmented, and metric-based approaches lacking a unifying perspective. We propose a unified framework grounded in functional PAC-Bayes theory, where meta-learning is reformulated as a bilevel optimization problem over a prior distribution over hypothesis spaces. Our key insight is that the inner-loop adaptation corresponds to conditional posterior inference given task-specific data, while the outer loop optimizes the meta-prior to minimize expected risk across tasks. We derive novel generalization bounds that decompose the meta-generalization error into task covariance, adaptation complexity, and meta-prior entropy terms, revealing fundamental trade-offs previously obscured by ad-hoc analyses. For the first time, we establish that optimal meta-learning requires balancing between task-specific adaptation fidelity and cross-task knowledge transfer, quantified through a new information-theoretic measure we term the adaptation-transfer coefficient. Experiments on synthetic and real meta-learning benchmarks validate our theoretical predictions, demonstrating that the derived bounds are significantly tighter than prior art. This work establishes the first cohesive theoretical paradigm for meta-learning, opening new directions for understanding and designing artificial intelligence systems capable of efficient few-shot learning.

We significantly advance the generalization theory for deep neural networks by establishing sharper non-vacuous bounds that better explain empirical observations in modern deep learning. The existing PAC-Bayes framework, while theoretically elegant, produces bounds that are often orders of magnitude loose for practical networks, failing to capture the implicit regularization effect of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We make three key contributions: First, we introduce a data-dependent posterior construction that adapts to the geometry of the loss landscape discovered during training, yielding substantially tighter posterior concentration. Second, we develop a novel analysis technique called trajectory margin counting that relates the SGD dynamics to the flatness of the final solution, providing a principled way to bound the expected generalization error. Third, we prove that the information bottleneck perspective emerges naturally from our framework, establishing a formal connection between compression and generalization. Our bounds achieve empirical calibration that is up to 10x tighter than previous state-of-the-art PAC-Bayes bounds on standard benchmarks including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Furthermore, our theory provides a theoretical justification for commonly observed phenomena such as double descent, revealing that it arises from the bias-variance tradeoff in posterior selection. This work substantially narrows the gap between theory and practice in understanding deep network generalization.

We introduce CausalNet, a fundamentally novel neural architecture paradigm that integrates causal reasoning directly into representation learning, moving beyond traditional correlation-based approaches. Current deep learning systems learn statistical associations that are brittle under distribution shift, lacking the ability to generalize under intervention or reason about counterfactuals. CausalNet addresses this limitation by implementing a differentiable causal graph module that operates alongside standard neural network components, enabling the system to learn representations that encode both observational patterns and causal structures. The architecture comprises three novel components: a structural causal model encoder that learns causal relationships from data, an intervention-aware representation module that produces invariant features across environments, and a counterfactual reasoning engine that enables hypothetical reasoning about alternative scenarios. We develop a scalable training procedure using variational inference that jointly optimizes predictive performance and causal structure recovery. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that CausalNet achieves superior out-of-distribution generalization compared to standard methods, maintains interpretable causal structures, and enables accurate counterfactual predictions. Applications in healthcare, scientific discovery, and autonomous systems showcase the practical impact of this new learning paradigm. CausalNet represents a paradigm shift toward more robust and interpretable artificial intelligence systems capable of causal reasoning.

We present EfficientFormerV3, a significantly improved vision transformer architecture that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through novel design principles for high-resolution vision tasks. While vision transformers have demonstrated remarkable performance across visual recognition benchmarks, their computational complexity remains prohibitive for high-resolution applications such as autonomous driving and medical imaging. EfficientFormerV3 introduces three key architectural innovations: First, a dynamic resolution adaptation mechanism that automatically adjusts token density based on local information content, reducing computation by 40% while maintaining accuracy. Second, a decomposed attention mechanism with localizedglobal interaction that captures both fine-grained details and long-range dependencies more effectively than existing approaches. Third, an adaptive skip connection structure that dynamically controls gradient flow based on training progress, enabling more stable optimization and better convergence. We develop an efficient implementation with kernel fusion and memory-efficient attention that achieves 3x speedup over previous methods on edge devices. Extensive evaluations on ImageNet, COCO, and ADE20K demonstrate that EfficientFormerV3 outperforms prior efficient vision transformers by 2-3% while maintaining comparable computational costs. The system achieves 84.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with only 4.2G FLOPs, establishing new state-of-the-art results. Pretrained models and code are publicly available, facilitating adoption in resource-constrained real-world applications.
